speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have waited for some time to be able to contribute to the debate on this piece of legislation which, if passed, will have the effect of privatizing the national energy company of Canada, in effect, Petro-Canada.
Petro-Canada legislation was passed in days gone by because the government of the day felt that it was in the best interest of the Canadian public to have a window on the energy market. There used to be a feeling in this country that the resources of the nation belonged to the people of the nation, no matter where they lived. In certain areas such as energy supply and security of supply it was important that the government, through programs or departments or in this particular case through a Crown corporation, have some input and a window on that particular aspect of Canadian sovereignty.
Through the years Petro-Canada has played a very important role in energy development in this country. It started with a lot of criticism from members opposite. It came in at a time when the government of the day felt that it was important to do so. This country has been blessed with a great energy resource, oil and gas, particularly in our western provinces and off the Atlantic coast, although that is not as fully developed as we would like it to be. There was a responsibility of the government to ensure that the Canadian interest was paramount in the development of that particular resource. That was in keeping with the way we used to think about this country. Many of us on this side still think that way, that this country is here for all of us and that it is the job of government to manage, as best as it can, those resources to the benefit of all Canadians.
I want to speak to these three amendments, but I feel I have to give a bit of background. When the Minister of State for Privatization came in with this latest scheme to try to take away something that was uniquely Canadian called Petro-Canada, he met with a lot of criticism. I know that many editorial writers, such as Geoffrey Simpson and many at The Globe and Mail and other newspapers from coast to coast, including some of the western papers in places like Alberta, said that this government was proceeding with a plan of privatization of a very necessary Crown corporation, one whose history, I will agree, was very controversial, especially in parts of western Canada. Maybe some of that was for the
right reasons, but perhaps this was not the right time to pursue this particular policy.
If we go back to the late 1970s, particularly 1979, we see that the previous Conservative government, when the right hon. member for Yellowhead was Prime Minister, had a different position on the national energy corporation, PetroCan, every second week. Those Conservatives were going to do away with it during the campaign. Then they came into power and they were not going to do away with it. They were going to privatize it; then they were going to abolish it. They were going to restrict it; then they were going to restructure it because they did not know what in the name of goodness to do.
At one point the current Minister for International Trade, after he was elected to this House in a by-election, took a tour of the west. He was one of those people who thought it was absolutely crazy that we had a company called Petro-Canada in the energy industry.
Mr. Speaker, do you know what happened? It was like the conversion on the road to Damascus. He got back in this place, and he could not say enough good about Petro-Canada and the important role it was playing in ensuring energy self-sufficiency in this country. He loved it. He could not say enough about it.
The current Governor General, in his former capacity as minister in this House, flip-flopped a number of times. When he was a minister, when he had some responsibilities in this place, particularly to the energy sector, he did not quite know what he stood for at any point in time.
We see that members of the government have almost been obsessed with Petro-Canada. In the beginning they got into typical Tory rhetoric that, if it cannot be done efficiently in the private sector, the public sector has no right to participate. That is typical Tory philosophy. We have seen it, particularly so in the last few days while they go in like a demolition derby and break apart national institutions such as CBC. They have gutted VTA. I listened with interest to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications today saying something which I am sure the minister of energy or the minister of privatization could have just as easily said about this particular bill on Petro-Canada. He said: "We had to cut it to make it better". It is like saying that we
December 6, 1990

have to kill you to cure you. That is basically what they are doing here.
The amendments that are before us right now dealing with Petro-Canada are important amendments. Canadians believe that our energy sector is one that has implications on our sovereignty. In the east coast of this country we have to rely on imported oil, gas, and crude oil even though this country is a net exporter of oil. Petro-Canada has played a major role in the development of Hibernia. It has played a major role in the Syncrude projects in western Canada. It has taken the leading edge because Petro-Canada's mandate was to look after the interests of Canadians, not to look after the interests of those in the corporate boardrooms in New York or over in some capital of Europe.
The amendments that we have before us are very important because of this crazy piece of legislation. I find it very difficult to listen to the minister of privatization at the best of times, but I tried very hard to listen to him because I figured that maybe there were some pearls of wisdom.
The only pearl of wisdom I could find was one that I had to sift through the sheets on: the reason it is going forward with the privatization of Petro-Canada at this point in time. When we have a major crisis in the Persian Gulf, when the very supply of crude oil to Atlantic Canada and other places is in question, and when Canadians once again are getting concerned about having a window in the energy sector so that they can direct and develop the energy sector, out of the blue the government, after many abortive attempts to do something with Petro-Canada-goodness knows what it wants to do; I am not sure-came in with a bill to privatize it.
One would have to come to the conclusion, after listening to the minister and watching what is happening across this country to Tory fortunes, that this bone was thrown out as a diversion for some caucus members, particularly the western caucus, who were getting their butts kicked solidly because of their support of this government's crazy GST, which has put them at 7 per cent in the polls. They will do anything for a diversion. I think this Petro-Canada privatization legislation at this point is such a diversion.
Government Orders
The minister opposite laughs. I think it is a nervous laugh. I do not think it is a belly laugh. I have seen a lot of ministers on the other side of the House doing a lot of nervous laughs the last little while. Every time a piece of legislation comes in that the Canadian public does not want, they all get the giggles over there. They say: "Gee, isn't it funny? The opposition is getting up and telling us the truth. It is telling us that we are doing something again that the public doesn't want". It is like a siege mentality, particularly on this bill. They really believe that everybody in the country is wrong and they are right. If they just put their faith in Brian, at some point in time everything will come out fine and smelling like roses. That is what they believe over there. It is little wonder they get kind of giddy at times.
The proposed amendments which we are speaking to today are important. If this government is going to pursue this crazy policy at the very time the people of Canada are seeing the energy reserves and resources as a national resource that can affect our sovereignty as a nation, they are going too far with it.
These amendments simply try to point out some difficulties. The motion that has been put forward by my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River, who has done a tremendous job, an absolutely phenomenal job of exposing this government for what it is and for what it is trying to do in the energy sector, shows that the government is bankrupt on policies. It does not have an national energy policy and wants to base everything on the marketplace. If it can be sold to the highest bidder it does not matter if it is a Canadian resource, just get rid of it. Get a few bucks in the coffers. If we cannot manage the economy, we cannot manage the government, we certainly need more money in the coffers. Forget about preserving and managing a national resource such as energy, oil and gas, for the benefit of everybody.
If the government wanted to do something perhaps it could have brought in some amendments to Petro-Canada to make sure that Petro-Canada was serving the interests of the consumers and the producers in western Canada.
The particular amendment, Motion No. 19, put forward by my colleague, who has piloted this legislation for us on this side of the House, the member for Scarborough-Rouge River who has done a great job, basically

December 6, 1990
Government Orders
says that the effect of this would be to prevent the ownership of shares in Petro-Canada while the Government of Canada still has shares.
What he is clearly trying to do is keep the government from an embarrassing situation where it will probably have some banana republic somewhere in the nether-nether land come in and see what a great deal Petro-Canada is and they can actually get a handle on Canadian energy reserves and resources. We just do not want the government to have other people in the energy sector and across the world sitting down comparing this government to one of those small banana republics because in this case that banana republic and its administrators will look a heck of a lot better than this government would.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that over the last number of months I have never felt so depressed and distressed about the welfare and good order of my country and its survival, its independence and sovereignty and nationhood, as I have under this government, and I have been here under several governments.
I must say to be fair that the present Conservative government and the Prime Minister have accomplished some things. Their main one is that they have contributed more to anger and outrage, alienation, than any other government since Confederation if not before.
Mr. Speaker, you can make a list as long as your arm, whether it was the Crow rate, the at and east rates, the two-price system on grain, whether it was the post office, VIA Rail, Petro-Canada, or anything else they have privatized. All they have done is remove from our society and our country the kind of things that kept us together and working. Of course, the CBC yesterday was just as bad a tragedy.
I would not mind if it could not help it, if it did not know better. It is when the government works at it that I get angry and depressed.
Motion No. 2A states that the chairman and members of the board must be Canadian residents. Well, Sir, I would rather they had to be Canadian citizens, but residents if they qualify under the appropriate regulation I guess is better than nothing. So I will buy that.
Motion No. 14A changes the limit of foreign ownership from 25 per cent to 1 per cent. I will buy that, too. If we had to compromise somewhere in between that, well, let's talk it over.
I want to quote the present minister of privatization-I am sorry he had to step out for a minute-because in the late unlamented nine months of the Clark government in 1979, he took great pains to emphasize the Canadian ownership line.
On December 11, 1979, at page 2255 of Hansard he is quoted as saying:
-only eligible Canadians-eligible Canadians-should be permitted to own shares in Petro-Canada and only eligible Canadians-Canadians, I repeat-should be entitled to buy shares in the after-market. I have stated many times that the shares must go to and remain in Canadian hands.
I do not know what happened to him since then, because obviously he knew better in 1979. In fact, he was applauded when he made that statement in the House. I do not know what happened to him. He was not on the road to Damascus. He was on the road to Sodom and Gomorrah since then.
There is something else I want to point out. I hate to use these words. Anything that impinges upon and hurts, that cuts down Canadian independence, sovereignty and nationhood, that destroys many decades of traditional behaviour by Canadians to be something more than and different from other countries-particularly our neighbour to the south-is a betrayal. We have adopted and implemented measures and laws in Canada that are unique.
Some are the envy of many other countries. I will not go into a long list of them. Anybody who flies in the face of that-I am prepared to make changes in accordance with that history-I have to say and I do not want to but I will, I call that nothing more than traitorous behaviour. It is a betrayal even of the present Conservative members' forefathers in Parliament; Mr. Diefenbaker and Sir John A. will be rolling over. Maybe they are now, I have no way of knowing.
They sure as heck would not have stood for this. No way. I am not one noted for applauding Mrs. Thatcher, the former Prime Minister of Great Britain, but even in her privatizations, and there were a bunch of them, she

always kept a back-up provision so that if the privatized company misbehaved, she could correct it.
Of 10 companies she privatized, she kept what is called "a golden share", only one share. That one share allowed her and her government to over-rule any privatized corporation from doing something that in her view and in her government's view was not in the national interest. She kept that golden share for a good reason. History and experience in our country and that of the United Kingdom have shown that if you turn a private corporation-whether it is multinational or national-loose to operate on their own, without any checks and balances, they are going to do what is best for them in the first place. What is best for their country takes second place, if that high. In fact, it probably takes third place. They will put the interests of the shareholders in second place. The country in which they have the privilege-not the right-to do business, takes a lower priority.
I do not understand why the minister will not accept amendments. Maybe he will. I hope I am wrong, but I do not think he will do the things outlined in these three amendments.
The third amendment would prohibit a foreign government or an agency of a foreign government, be it a Crown corporation, board, or anything else, from owning any Petro-Canada shares. Surely that makes some sense, which the minister was heckling my colleague about.
It makes common sense, because you are either master in your own house, or you are not. If you are going to turn this over to anyone and everyone to do with as they please for the sake of making a buck, and to hell with the welfare and the good order of Canada and its people, then they have no business here. They lose their privileges. No corporation has the right to exploit resources and ignore the welfare and good order of my country.
I hope these amendments will pass and that we can get on to the other ones.

Mr. Speaker, before I make some remarks on the proposed amendments to Bill C-84, respecting the privatization of Petro-Canada, I would like to bring to the attention of the House one matter because it is a day of commemorating tragedies.
Government Orders
We have heard our colleagues in the House remark on the sad events which took place last year in Montreal on December 6.1 just want to remind the House of another very tragic event that took place in the city of Halifax 73 years ago on this same date, December 6. That was the Halifax explosion which resulted in the tragic loss of 1,600 lives and over 9,000 injuries. Over 20 per cent of the population of Halifax was directly affected by that tragic event.
Without detracting in any way from the remarks made on the tragic event in Montreal, I think it is well to record that again in the House and remind members of it. I hope 83 years from now we will again remember both events because they are sad days for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, may I now address Bill C-84 which before the House of Commons.
I would like to deal with the facts because we hear a great deal of rhetoric about national corporations like Petro-Canada, as we hear about Air Canada, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and so on, and it is now said without feeling, I hope. I respect the views of those who regard these organizations as national institutions which should be preserved at whatever cost. It is simply that I do not share that view.
I believe these are utilitarian organizations which perform a function and if we can perform the function in a way that saves taxpayers' money, that provides services, then we should look at those possibilities. That is, indeed, what we are doing with Bill C-84. We believe that Petro-Canada has served its function. It can continue as a utilitarian corporation providing services to Canada in another way.
For those reasons I want to deal with some facts, because when Petro-Canada was created, it was intended to give a window on the industry for reasons that occurred at that time. But let us look at some of the evolutionary aspects of Petro-Canada. When they took over Canadian Petrofina, what happened? Vast amounts of money were spent on that acquisition. They were never properly accounted for. We do not know who received the benefits of those extensive payments. We never did get a clear financial picture.
As the member well knows, the courts have made decisions on this subject. The files are closed. They are sealed. They are not available to Parliamentarians, nor to the Auditor General. So we do not know what really is

December 6, 1990
Government Orders
the history of Petro-Canada. We do not know what chicanery took place among supporters of the Liberal Party who were shareholders of Petrofina and who were engaged in this exercise.
It is not as if Petro-Canada had a clean history among Canadians and in the business field. It might have been conceived in good faith, but it evolved into infamy. That is why I want to look at Petro-Canada, in terms of whether it has performed any function for the people of Canada. They may ask: "What has it done for Canadians?"
If one was to go to a Petro-Canada dealer, one would find that he enters into the same kind of contract with the corporation as any other commercial petroleum dealer does. He is required to buy tires, batteries, and accessories from the company at inflated prices.
I can tell you of a specific case, Mr. Speaker, where a Petro-Canada dealer was forced to buy window washing material at a price higher than it was available for at Zellers. As you know, Zellers makes the boast that it has the lowest prices, but it is a retail outfit. The Petro-Canada dealer could get a lower price at a commercial retail store than he could from Petro-Canada. Why? Because Petro-Canada was profiteering at the expense of its dealers. In that respect it is no different, in its operation and its management, from any other company. Members opposite know that the government, Liberal or Conservative, did not ever interfere in the day-to-day management of the company. It was left to function like any other petroleum corporation.
I assure you that if you go to a Petro-Canada station anywhere in Canada, you will pay the same price that you pay at other stations. You will get the same lack of guarantee, if you get repairs, and you will have the same kinds of arguments. Do not tell me, as a Canadian consumer, that Petro-Canada has done anything for me. It has functioned simply as a commercial corporation. The window that we thought was there is not there. Thus, the raison d'etre for Petro-Canada has been diminished, if not eliminated altogether.
Let me get on to some of the other rhetoric that we have heard in the House of Commons. There is a great fear of foreign takeovers. Every time the New Democratic Party members get upset about kind of a transaction, they bring in the myth, the bogey, of the foreigners who are going to come in and take over Canada. That makes an interesting point because a business writer for The Daily News of Halifax, one John McLeod, has made this point about our friends in the New Democratic Party. In an article today, December 6, 1990 he states, and I quote:
It's instructive to note the difference between New Democratic Party economic policy as espoused by an out-of-power federal leader, and the economic policy of the new NDP government in Ontario.
Let me tell you what has happened in Ontario, Mr. Speaker. Notwithstanding this great fear of foreign takeovers, and notwithstanding "Canada for Canadians", "Let us own all of our corporations", "Let us have restrictions on ownership", and "Let us make ownership available only to Canadians", what happens when the Ontario government under Premier Bob Rae gets its first test? It approves the sale of Consumer's Gas to British Gas, PLC. Why did it approve the sale of a Canadian corporation in the energy field to a foreign corporation? Because it was in the best interests of the people of Ontario, so it said.
All of the ideology that it spoke of in the House in this very debate, that went out of the window because it had to face the practical problem of: What are we going to do? We have a request from a foreign company, British Gas, to take over a Canadian company, Consumer's Gas, so what are we going to do? Are we going to decide it on ideology, like our federal friends do? No. No ideology for us. It is out the window. We are in government now. We have to decide it on the practicalities of the case and the practicalities of the case dictate that the right decision is to approve the sale. That is what Bob Rae did and I do not know what the New Democratic leader is going to say about it when they meet. They had better get together.
I hear they have a television set over there in the lobby to keep on eye on the legislature. The reason they have two television sets is because they know they are saying two different things in the two different places and they are trying to bring them together. The ideology they espouse in this Chamber clashes with the practical facts. It was right and proper to allow British Gas to take over Consumer's Gas. That is the decision the Ontario government made.
December 6, 1990

The Financial Times has some advice for Bob Rae, as well as John McLeod. It is saying, "Listen, Mr. Bob Rae, listen Mr. New Democratic Party and Mrs. New Democratic Party, you will have to find a better way to preserve domestic control of strategic companies and sectors." There must be a better way. It has nothing to do with shareholdings. It has nothing to do with ownership. It has to do with legislative control. You can control corporations, as Bob Rae now knows, by legislation. You can make corporations do what is in the public interest by legislation. You do not have to worry about ownership.
We found out with Petro-Canada that it does not make a bit of difference. Petro-Canada explores where Petro-Canada wants to explore. Petro-Canada sells what Petro-Canada wants to sell. Petro-Canada charges what Petro-Canada wants to charge. It did not do us any good in the Parliament of Canada or across Canada to have this window in the industry. We might as well recognize it and let the commercial forces take control as they have in the past.
I hope the New Democratic members have learned a lesson from their friend, Bob Rae. I hope they will be practical. Ideology is nice, but let us face facts.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I feel very much like the previous New Democratic speaker and the member for Winnipeg- Transcona did in speaking on this privatization bill. Having seen what the Conservative government has done to the country and to its fundamental institutions over the last several years, a lot of people in the country have serious and grave doubts as to whether the country is going to continue to exist for much longer after the systematic attack that has been taken on the fundamental institutions of Canada.
Before I get into the actual detail of the amendments and the bill itself, I would like to talk a bit about the comments that have been made about ideology by the last few speakers on the Conservative side. It might be
Government Orders
worth-while to recall to those speakers that the New Democratic Party has not nationalized a single corporation or set up a single corporation federally in the country.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as the Tories admitted in the debate yesterday and in previous days, was set up by the R. B. Bennett Tory government back in the 1920s and 1930s. Canadian National Railways, back in 1923, was set up, I believe, by a Liberal government of the day. Air Canada was set up as one of the projects of C. D. Howe, a Liberal cabinet minister.
In looking at the provincial story, Mr. Speaker, you will recall as a member from Alberta, that the Pacific Western Airlines was at one time nationalized by Peter Lougheed, one of the great free enterprisers of Canada.
In my recollection of British Columbia history, B.C. Electric, which is an offshoot of the Power Corporation of Canada, was nationalized by W. A. C. Bennett and his Social Credit Party, the so-called free enterprise party of British Columbia, which was formed back in the early 1950s when the Liberals and the Tories jumped into bed with each other and nationalized the power company.
The simple fact is that Crown corporations are not set up on the basis of ideology. The vast majority of Crown corporations in Canada were set up because the government of the day, regardless of political stripe, recognized a need that was not being fulfilled by the private sector. It said that in the absence of investment by the private sector, the government has to take action in order to develop the country, move the country ahead, and achieve the kind of progress that we are looking for. As a result, those governments of those days-whether Conservative, Liberal, Social Credit, or even New Democrat-got involved in the nationalization or the establishment of Crown corporations.
We did the same thing in British Columbia when we were in government. We set up an insurance corporation. That insurance corporation in fact brought a financial centre to Vancouver based on hundreds of millions of dollars of premiums that in the past went to Zurich, New York, or Hartford, Connecticut. We repatriated that money to the benefit of British Columbians and it was the basis of a financial centre in Vancouver that has grown and thrived to this present day. It was done strictly on a pragmatic basis. It has nothing to do with ideology.

Government Orders
I remember meeting with the minister of agriculture for Sweden, Mats Hellstrom, who is playing a role in the GATT talks in Brussels this very day. He advised me that when the democratic socialist government was in power in Sweden, it did not nationalize a single corporation and its policy was opposed to it. It preferred that the corporations operated in a tightly regulated free enterprise sector.
However, when the right-wing government took over from the social democrats, it nationalized some corporations that were held by a lot of its friends and financial supporters who had gone broke. They persuaded the right-wing government to take those corporations over and the taxpayers ended up bailing out those corporations.
In some cases, that is exactly what happened here in Canada. The government of the day recognized the need of some of its financial donors to have these corporations taken off their hands. After all, Canadian National was not nationalized. Its private operators bankrupted it and then the government was forced to take it over.
The same thing happened, as my colleague reminded me, in British Columbia with the B.C. rail system, the former Pacific Great Eastern Railway. When the railway sold off all the land grants that were given to it by the province and ran the railway into the ground because it started from nowhere and ended nowhere, the government of the day took over the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and completed it from terminus to terminus. Now it operates as one of the great railways of the country, performing a service to developing the central and northern part of British Columbia and shipping our lumber out into export markets. It was done strictly for pragmatic reasons in some cases, but also it was done by Liberal and Tory governments to bail out their bankrupt supporters and to use taxpayers' funds to take over these corporations.
I am more concerned right now about what this government is doing to our national institutions. I am concerned about the destruction of the post office as a community centre and as a means of communication that represents Canada in virtually every single community in every single riding in the country. There is the destruction of Canada's national airline, Air Canada, which was sold off by the Conservative government through a
privatization process and now Air Canada is in the process of selling off its assets, its share of an aircraft leasing corporation based in Ireland, selling off its aircraft, cutting down on its services, and cutting down on the communities that it serves in the country. It is now in the private sector and it does not have to have a commitment to the Canadian people and to each and every community in Canada.
The government has done the same thing with VIA Rail. Railways were the first things that brought the country together. When my family came from Ireland in 1819 to the country, they came as many Irish people did, to build the railways in the country that were the initial ties that bound the provinces and ultimately the country together. Now, this government has severed those ties. It has broken up the rail system and this major institution of Canada that brought the country together, and continues to hold the country together, is now in jeopardy as a result of what the Conservative government is doing.
I do not think the Conservative government is privatizing Petro-Canada because it is going to improve the corporation's operations. I think it is going to operate the same way as they have instructed it to operate now. If it is gouging people, it is going to continue to do so, but it is only doing so now because it has been instructed or permitted by the Conservative Party in government to do so, so that the people of Canada will lose their respect for the institution of a national petroleum company and refuse to support it.
Basically what they are doing is following their ideological bent. This is a new ideological bent. This is not the old Conservatism of John A. Macdonald, R. B. Borden, or Meighen, all of whom had as their goal and as their objective the progress of Canada and the progress of its institutions.
This is Conservatism that derives itself from the new-right Republicanism of the United States, a Republicanism exemplified by the presidency of Ronald Reagan. He talked about fighting the deficit, yet he ran the deficit of the United States higher than any other president, any other political party in history. He talked about privatization. He talked about deregulation and we know exactly what happened to the thrifts and the savings and loans institutions in the United States. Deregulation meant that every crook and gouger who
December 6, 1990

could get into the savings and loan industry could gouge money out of the savings of citizens in the United States, spend it on useless projects, and totally enrich themselves at the expense of the United States. That is precisely what this party and its friends in private business are doing.
They are draining the cup of Canada. They are draining the assets of government, and they are destroying the fundamental institutions of this country, and that is exactly the meaning of this bill.

If you wanted to nationalize something and they thought that would be popular, that is precisely what they would do. Ideology had nothing to do with the way they made a government function. If it needed to be done, they would do it.

There is an interjection here about the Liberals leaving a big debt. That is true. As I went through the committee deliberations on these amendments, one of the things that struck me was when you search for a reason for why this government is trying to privatize this particular corporation at the moment, one eludes you.
As you read through the deliberations in committee, it seems that a pretty comprehensive argument was being made that this would be a sensible corporation to retain, that there were things that could be done with Petro-Canada that would assist us in terms of making the environment of Canada a better place, and that we had concerns now about our own energy needs. I disregard totally the old cliche that you need a window on the industry because it seems that one of the faults of Petro-Canada is that that is about all it ever was-people standing at a window looking at the private sector at work.
There is a lot more potential that was there that should have been realized. One of the things that surprises me about these amendments that are before us now is that this appears to be the last little thread. Even Maggie Thatcher on her worst day when she was selling off the assets of the British government, at least had the common sense and the common decency to say that at least it ought to be retained in the hands of people from this country.
This government seems to reject that notion. I do not know why it would be so anxious to reject that. I am not certain at all why it would take a business decision at the moment. It appears to me, at least, to be a very bad business decision. In the middle of an energy crisis, it seems to me you would look at something like Petro-Canada as an asset, not a liability. It seems to be making money. That is my definition of a good business proposition.
As strange a notion as this is, there are those who believe in the world of corporate socialism. I am not one of them. Obviously the members opposite on the govern-

Government Orders
ment side believe in that kind of socialism. They believe that all taxpayers in Canada ought to fund the corporate sector somehow.
If you look at the government's tax policies, it certainly does that. If you look at this particular bill, it seems to follow in the same vein. The government feels that somehow the people of Canada had an obligation to set up an oil company; to bear all of the costs, trials and tribulations it would take to get that set up, then at the point where that company might make some money, it ought to be sold off to the private sector. I do not understand that.
Petro-Canada seems to be a corporation that has developed a role for itself. It is certainly not the role that I would want it to play. I have a much higher set of expectations for it than the government does.
It seems to me that during the committee proceedings members from all three parties and people from Petro-Canada accepted the notion that we could do some very good things with this oil company, that this would give us an opportunity to develop things that are environmentally sound, to make our people more conscious of their energy use. It would make sure that we had a constant supply of energy. We certainly have gone to great pains all across the country to see that there is a network in place to do something for this corporation and for this country; that it would ensure our constant energy supply.
I do not know why the government would reject amendments such as these. It seems to me that they are minimal at best. It seems to me they simply address that this is a company which the people of Canada put a lot of money into. I do not think anyone has an accurate total of what the total taxpayer investment is in Petro-Canada, but it has to be huge.
It does seem that there is a vendetta here; that this current government still is chasing Pierre Elliott Trudeau around. It might gather up some sympathy from me on that, but it does seem to me that it has not used common sense. Here is an opportunity to retain a corporation with great potential that is beginning to do something useful, and it ought to try to retain it. I am not sure that it is their ideology. I am not sure that that is the right word. This is certainly Tories of a different stripe at work than the ones that I am used to.
The amendments that are before us are amendments that ought to be supported by all members. They are certainly minimal. They are amendments which attempt to keep some Canadian connection in Petro-Canada. It seems to me that this government, even in privatizing it, wants to do that.
I read the proceedings of the committee and I looked for the arguments that said why the government would not accept these amendments. To tell you the truth, I did not find them. Perhaps they are here. Perhaps during the remainder of this debate, one of the things the minister might do for us is instead of standing in his place and giving us a little diatribe about ideology, he could address the amendments that are before us and provide the House with some rationale as to why the government is not prepared to accept the amendments that are currently before the House.

I am very pleased to see that the Minister of State for Privatization is in the House. Perhaps I could comment with regard to what the minister said in 1979.
The Conservative minority government at that time was in an election. It talked about privatizing Petro-Can-ada, and half way through the election campaign decided that the Canadian people did not want that, and so reversed its decision.
I will start off by stating what the late Tommy Douglas, New Democratic Party Leader, said in the House of Commons on November 15, 1978:
Every person who has looked at the situation knows that any
industry which controls the energy resources of a nation has its fingers

Petro-Canada itself represents the clear choice, in his words:
- the choice in this country is whether or not we are going to develop the petroleum resources of Canada for the benefit of Canadian people, or whether we are going to continue to be the economic colony of which our vital energy resources are owned and controlled by foreign multinational corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I am one of the people who has had a life-long fascination with the oil industry, having grown up in one of the
original oil patches in Alberta in the Black Diamond Timer Valley oilfield. I can remember, as a child growing up, that the whole discussion in that community focused on the development of our oil and gas industry in Canada. I lived there at the time the Leduc oilfield was discovered. The shift from the town was almost wholesale as it moved from the Timer Valley Black Diamond area to Leduc.
Even at that time people were concerned about who was controlling our industry, who was going to benefit from our industry. Would it be foreign oil companies? Would it be the average resident of Alberta? Would it be the Canadian public with reliable, cheap energy resources? Or, would it be turned over to the free enterprise international marketplace?
Unfortunately, over the years a far too great percentage of our petroleum industry has been controlled by foreign capital and foreign investment, where the profits have been taken out of the country and where the decisions being made are being made not in the interests of Canadians, but in the interests of the profits of a foreign company.
Of all times for Canada to be surrendering its only instrument in policy in the petroleum industry, now could not be a worse time. Right now we are in the middle of the gulf crisis, and the gulf crisis is about oil. Anyone who thinks it is about anything else other than the control of oil fields is sadly mistaken.
Last winter I had the opportunity to spend two weeks in the gulf area, in the United Arab Emirates, another one of the Arab countries much like Kuwait. It is an oil producing country wherein the oil productivity is only benefiting a very select group of people; not the average person and not the workers of which 80 per cent are imported, but the wealthy sheikh families.
This is basically what we have done in this country, only we call them corporations. We have let the large multinational corporations control and direct our oil industry, not for Canadians but for the benefit of themselves.
We have a piece of legislation before the House that is bad. It is wrong. It is fundamentally wrong, particularly at this point in time. We are trying to get the government to show some reason, some understanding, and accept some amendments that would at least make sure that,

even if it were privatized, it would still be in the control of Canadians.
We are suggesting two or three amendments. First, the people on the board of directors must at least be residents of Canada; not even Canadians but at least residents of Canada so that hopefully the decisions will continue to be made in Canada, not in the boardrooms of the United States.
Second, we are suggesting that we must reduce the percentage of permissible foreign ownership. Right now under the present set-up we could end up with the effective control of Petro-Canada being outside Canada. If you have three foreign owned blocks, two of them with 10 per cent and one with 5 per cent, 25 per cent controlled by three co-ordinated companies that were foreign, and the rest of the shares dispersed across the Canadian public, with a 25 per cent block you could control that company effectively. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE AND SUPREME COURT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Peterborough for presenting his private members' bill, Bill C-210, to improve the extradition process. I have received comments from many people commending the hon. member for his perseverance on this issue and his over-all dedication to the cause of justice in Canada.
I regret the necessity to make amendments to our Extradition Act. As a Canadian, I am embarrassed that we have such a slow and cumbersome procedure, one that appears to allow foreign fugitives to languish in Canadian custody at Canadian expense, rather than face justice in their own country.

December 6, 1990
Private Members' Business
Many members of that public have become discouraged, disillusioned, and even mad about what they see about a lengthy and expensive process that seems to deny justice, rather than expedite it. For this reason, these amendments have been applauded by the media and public alike.
The hon. member for Peterborough did a good job of explaining what the bill accomplishes and how it can shorten the time from initial requests to final decision by up to a year and a half.
There has now been close to a month elapsed and, very briefly, I would like to go into how the extradition process works right now. To begin with, when an individual who is suspected or convicted of a crime in another country crosses a border into Canada, and authorities of that country become aware that he is here, they would make an official request to Canadian authorities to extradite him. The Canadian authorities would then have to ask a judge of a county or superior court to issue a warrant to arrest that fugitive and place him in detention before surrendering. The judge would issue that warrant if the other nation's conviction of the fugitive is proven or if the offence he is accused of in the other nation is an offence in Canada.
At this point, the individual may apply for a writ of habeas corpus to another superior court judge to be removed from prison. That is, in effect, to block the extradition. The individual at that point would be questioning his liability for extradition. A judgment would be issued on that writ of habeas corpus which the individual can then appeal to the court of appeal of the province he or she happens to be in. In this appeal hearing, there is no production of evidence, no witnesses, and no cross examination, but simply discussion of the legal issues. Assuming the appeal is denied, in the present system the individual can then request permission to appeal that decision to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The case would then, assuming it is upheld again, be referred to the Minister of Justice who must wait at least 15 days from the expiration of the date of the final appeal before indicating his or her decision as to whether or not to surrender the fugitive to the other nation's authorities.
It goes on, because the individual can then attempt to challenge the decision of the minister to surrender or extradite him.
The second stage of recourse is much narrower in scope. The individual may apply to the Federal Court and then appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal. If unsuccessful, the individual can ask permission to appeal that judgment to the Supreme Court of Canada again. This is an extraordinary remedy.
I do not want to comment on the specifics of the Charles Ng case, but it is significant to recognize the desire of the Minister of Justice to expedite a final decision in this case, which has been dragging on in the Canadian courts for far too long.
The minister has referred the appeal of the minister's decision directly to the Supreme Court, thereby significantly shortening the second level of appeal.
In future cases, we do not want the minister to have to make direct referrals. We want to improve the system. Bill C-210 does that by removing two levels of appeals, one to the provincial court and the other to the Supreme Court.
The minister since our last debate in this House has made a response to the report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. Quoting from that, she has offered serious consideration and discussion leading to a new act or significant amendments to the present law.
I applaud her decision, but I do not feel they should preclude the interim improvements such as those proposed in this bill. The study will take some time. We have the opportunity for action and improvements now. Passing this bill will signal our resolve to improve the Extradition Act and help restore some waning confidence in our justice system.
The minister's study may well offer more substantial improvements, but if we can act on this bill we will show our determination to tighten the system and make our country with its legal system less appealing to foreign fugitives.
I do not see any reason at all why this House should not unanimously agree with the principle in this bill and get on with it. In fact, if the New Democratic Party had not filibustered last month when the bill was first
December 6, 1990

introduced, it could have been off to committee and possibly even back here for third reading and approval today.
The principle in this bill has the support of tens of thousands of Canadians. From my own riding I presented thousands of signatures on petitions calling on the Government of Canada to do exactly what this bill proposes. These petitioners do not want Canada to become a haven for foreign fugitives from justice. I have not met or heard from a single Canadian who supports the status quo. These people want an indication that we are prepared to act, and act now.
It is important to keep in mind that the individuals affected by these amendments will still have the opportunity to appear before Canadian courts. They will still have due process available to them. An individual who is not a citizen of this country will still have their rights protected. They will still be entitled to have their cases heard and appealed.
This bill simply limits the number of those appeals and it will make Canada slightly less appealing as a haven for foreign fugitives.
I would also suggest that the average Canadian, and I include myself in this group, cannot comprehend why we have such a problem and why we allow it to continue. How can a non-Canadian charged, accused, or even convicted under the laws of another sovereign nation, tie up our legal system for five to six years.
Why are we willing to spend so much money and time to keep them from answering charges in their own country? I cannot answer, and I do not understand.
I am not a lawyer. However, my understanding of law has always been that the purpose of law is to establish order in society and to protect the values, safety and security of that society.
I would suggest that if the law goes too far in protecting the rights of the individual without requiring any responsibilities, there is a very real danger that the law is going to have the effect of destroying the very society that it sets out to protect.
That destruction starts when the members of society lose confidence in the law, begin to ridicule it and hold it up to contempt. This act and recent cases involving it are
Private Members' Business
one instance where to protect individual rights, we have allowed a situation where the law is attracting abuse and contempt. We cannot allow this to continue.
The present system takes too long. The chances of convicting a guilty person must reasonably decrease with the passage of time. It is wrong to allow someone to use the Canadian legal system to stall for time while witnesses' memories fade or witnesses move or die. Even more significant, while our system slowly moves, victims and victims' families wait for justice.
I am sure that we are all agreed that everyone is entitled to due process, but justice is not served by delaying resolution. The Canadian taxpayer is not served by allowing foreign fugitives to languish in Canadian jails at Canadian expense. Let us pass this bill.
Let us improve our system of extradition and show Canadians that we are reasonable; that we believe in and accept the need for due process; but also that we believe in the responsibility of the individual to answer for his or her actions and that we refuse to allow foreign fugitives to hide out in the Canadian judicial system. Let us approve this bill.

It deals with an area of law that a number of us in Parliament have been looking at very closely over the last year or two.
I recall in January of this year the former justice minister addressing the issue publicly as an item of very compelling public interest. On the one hand he had certain function quasi judicial to take care of which prevented him from speaking too much on the issue but, on the other hand, he had his public responsibilities here to the people of Canada and to us in the House of Commons.
Certain commitments were made at that time to address the area of the Extradition Act and the Fugitive Offenders Act. A few months later in the justice committee, the current justice minister and officials appeared and indicated that the matter was under study. We all know that the matter has been under study for a long time and it is still being studied and I, for one, cannot

December 6, 1990
Private Members' Business
figure out why approximately three statutes are taking so long to decipher and a solution so long to be generated.
The hon. member for Peterborough with this private member's bill has provided the House of Commons with an opportunity to address this problem area directly and concisely. I gather that if the bill is passed by members, it can go to either a legislative committee or the justice committee which would take a closer look at some of the administrative implications.
The way this area of law is structured now-it is not embarrassing to stand here because it is a public issue-if the public was truly aware of the duplications, the complications, the conflicts, the redundancies, the absurdities, in the four federal statutes that govern this area, people might be lined up at the front door here. I do not get a sense of good management here; I get a sense of terrible management and a lack of interest. I grant that there have been other public issues in the justice area, that have kept the justice minister busy like gun control, the Meech Lake Constitution process, the abortion issue and other very compelling national matters, but these provisions in the Extradition Act and the Fugitive Offenders Act, the Corrections Act, and the Immigration Act are starting to embarrass us and, as my friend, the hon. member for Red Deer, just mentioned, there are 25 or 30 million people in the state of California trying to figure out what 25 million people here in Canada are doing. They cannot figure out how someone who is a U.S. citizen can suddenly show up on our doorstep and camp out until we no longer have any use for him.
I have read the provisions of the Immigration Act which state very clearly that an individual who is incarcerated can be removed or deported, it is very simple, upon the expiration of the period of time which he must serve in an institution, and that is approximately two-thirds of one's sentence.
I do not want to mention the individual's name, there is not need to, it has been mentioned in the House, but why the immigration officials did not go to the penitentiary in which that convicted person was and have him dealt with at a deportation hearing the day after two-thirds of the sentence had passed, I do not know. Since that time we have been participating, along with him, in what has become a growth industry involving our legal aid system, our judicial system, up and down, back and
forth, to and from, the Supreme Court. This is costing us all money, not to mention the embarrassment. We do not seem to be able to move a body out of this country when it is obvious from our Immigration Act that we have the authority to do so. We just continue to sit back and do nothing.
We can remove an individual who has not committed a crime, but we cannot get rid of an individual who has committed a crime. This is an absurdity. I know in other parts of the world, if an individual of this type were to show up in another country and officials in that country were aware of it, that person would have a hearing. Depending on how the hearing turned out, the person would be taken to the airport and sent back home where he or she belongs.
People in this country are tired of providing safe haven to criminals. We do not mind being the haven to convention refugees under the United Nations Charter. We have done an admirable job and we are justifiably proud of what we have done. It has cost us dearly but we are happy to do that. But we are not happy to be a safe haven for criminals.
This particular bill gives us an opportunity, if I may use the term, on a fast-track basis, to take that narrow focus of extradition law, the focus of the difficulty we are having now, pass it at second reading, move it to a committee and then, hopefully, pass it into law and assist the justice officials and the Minister of Justice in completing this area of badly-needed homework.

This afternoon representatives of Victims of Violence, a fine organization in this city, telephoned some of the victims. I have always in my political career, when I talked to someone, tried to put myself in their position. I would like members of this House to put themselves in the position of the people who have lost loved ones, who do not know where their loved ones are, who have no idea where the bodies are hidden. They spoke to different people. I will name a few. They spoke to Richard and Sharon O'Connor in California, and they said they support the California stand. They spoke to Virginia and David Nestle, and they support the California stand. They spoke to Dwight Lola of Stapley and Joy Ireland, and they support the California resolution. They spoke to Roger and Marlene Geraldton and family, and they support the California resolution. I could go on and on. This is a very emotional issue.
Let us get to the mechanics of the bill that were very well explained by my colleague from Red Deer. The NDP does not like this bill. I congratulate the Liberal Party for supporting us on this. What we have here is the current extradition process: the extradition hearing and it moves to a writ of habeas corpus. From there it goes to an appeal, a relevant provincial court appeal. From there it goes to appeal to the Supreme Court. Then it goes to the Minister of Justice for a decision. The minister's decision is appealed then to the Federal Court Trials Division. Then it is appealed to the Federal Court of Canada Appeals Division. Then it is appealed to the Supreme Court, and they start over again. This is absolutely ridiculous. It has to be fast-tracked in some way.
All we are asking to do is to remove two parts. The NDP says: "We don't want these parts removed because you must have an appeal to the relevant provincial court of appeal". However, what I am informed is that when you take away that appeal you have to put something in its place. You have to put in an appeal to a three-judge tribunal.
We are not asking for a big thing. We are asking for a small step to make Canada have some respect in its laws. We have submitted in the third report of the justice committee four recommendations to the minister. I could read from it: "The committee has considered aspects of the law and the process of extradition", and so

Private Members' Business
on. We go on with four recommendations. The NDP says: "We support these recommendations".
However, our recommendations were not accepted at this time by the minister. The minister stated her reasons. She goes on to say in the conclusion as well: "The recommendations raise broader issues which require thorough consideration". Fine, let us take one small step. Let us support this private member's initiative.
We all remember the times when private members did not have a say in this House. They did not have very much say at all. The McGrath commission changed that, and now we have private members' bills that pass. In the last Parliament we had five private members' bills of great significance that passed. In this Parliament I want to see one pass, and I want to see this one pass.
I know that the NDP caucus members have great deep feelings for these victims. I know that they feel as deeply as I do. However, they cannot take a stand against this bill in all good conscience and I can tell you why. I have in my possession a letter from the former justice critic of the New Democratic Party, the member for Burnaby- Kingsway. I would like to read this letter into the record. The letter is to George Bears, Director, Victims of Violence. It reads:
Dear Mr. Bears:
My colleague, Audrey McLaughlin, has passed your memo on to me expressing your concern about the lengthy process of extradition in the Charles Ng case.
I am sorry to mention the case, but it is in the letter. It continues:
I share your concern on this question. I believe that current provisions of the Extradition Act lead to inordinate delays in extradition. There are too many steps in the appeal process. The legal requirement that a fugitive who has been accused of an offence in Canada (not the extradition offence) or who has been convicted and sentenced for a crime in Canada, cannot be surrendered until after he or she has either been acquitted or has finished serving the sentence imposed by the Canadian court is unacceptable. Indeed, in contrast with this mandatory wording, the treaty with the United States provides that surrender in such a situation is discretionary.
This was from the justice critic of the New Democratic Party. In his last paragraph he writes:
In light of these weaknesses in the Act, I am preparing a Private Member's bill to respond to these concerns and to tighten the Act. I
will be pleased to send you a copy of my bill when it has been
drafted.
I have never seen it. I have checked. There is no such bill, but there is a bill from the member for Peterborough. I ask for the NDP to support this bill, put it to a vote, refer it to the justice committee, and let us get things done in this Parliament.

Touche, touche. That is right, but this bill is dealing with the future. That is what we are dealing with, so let us deal with this bill.
The process needs streamlining. We all agree with that. There is a solution to that. The solution is the report of the justice committee, signed by the member for Mississauga West, who was the last speaker for the Conservatives. As the member said in his own speech, it was not accepted by the Minister of Justice. That was a three-stage procedure.
Now the member for Peterborough comes along and introduces a two-stage procedure. Does the member for Mississauga West really believe that the Minister of Justice is going to accept a two-stage procedure when she thought a three-stage procedure was too fast? Come on now, let us not have hypocrisy here. Come on, let us be honest with the Canadian people. Let us quit scoring
December 6, 1990

cheap politics. This is cheap politics. The solution is in the justice committee report. We want a streamlined system. We want a legal system.
Let me tell you about the flaw in the bill. I will go through the procedure, as did the member who first spoke suggested. Right now there is an extradition hearing. There is an appeal by a writ of habeas corpus. That is not anywhere in our law. That is a common law right. Then there is an appeal from the habeas corpus. The reason there is an appeal from the habeas corpus is that the habeas corpus is heard by a judge at the same court level that hears extradition cases. It could even be the same judge. That is why there is an appeal from that. That is why, if this bill goes through, the courts are liable to declare the bill unconstitutional. The courts are liable to declare the bill as violating the charter of rights.
You ask me what is my authority for that. My authority is the legal opinion of the justice department of the federal government which states exactly that on page 6 of the report.

No, it is not different entirely. It is exactly on that. It makes sense too. It makes sense because how can you not restrict an appeal from a habeas corpus? If you start restricting that, you will be in some deep constitutional problems. What will happen-I won't mention the name Ng-and hopefully it will not happen is that if another fugitive comes here and gets a smart lawyer, the lawyer will go to court on this bill and delay it even further. If we pass this bill we will be in a bigger legal morass. We will be in deeper.
What we have to do is get smart. We have to put the onus on the Minister of Justice and follow the recommendations of the justice committee, which was a unanimous report that made legal sense. It streamlined the process.
Let me go back again in this process. Right now there is an extradition hearing, a writ of habeas corpus, an appeal from that, then an appeal to the Supreme Court, then a decision of the minister, and then there has been appeals. That was what Mr. Ng was doing, appealing that to the Federal Court and to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court is going to make a decision soon and likely, whichever way it decides, that will eliminate about
Private Members' Business
three steps because that case will already be decided; the issue being: How does the charter of rights apply if you want to send someone out of the country where there is capital punishment in the other jurisdiction or there is harsh and unconscionable punishment? That will be decided. If we were smart, we would wait for the Supreme Court. The decision is pending now. We should wait for that decision. That will likely eliminate three parts of the procedure. Then what will we be left with? The member for Peterborough's bill, which will be an extradition hearing, a quick habeas corpus, and then out of the country. That is too fast, and it may be illegal and unconstitutional.
There are all kinds of future cases we may have on extradition. Remember Leonard Pelletier? He is now languishing in a jail in the States through trumped-up evidence, which legal scholars now agree was a pretty unfair hearing. We have to get a procedure that is streamlined but fair. My colleagues and I do not like what is going on with Mr. Ng and so on in those kinds of cases. We want to streamline the procedure, but we want it to be constitutional and legal.
I said there was hypocrisy. The government put up more speakers than the NDP. The Liberals have almost put up more speakers than the NDP, but we are getting blamed and they are putting up the speakers. The minister, who told me personally that she was against the bill, and the parliamentary secretary, who is against the bill but does not want to speak, will put it off to this committee and then prorogue Parliament. That will get the best of both worlds. They will claim to the victims of violence that they let it go through. Then they will claim to the justice department and the lawyers that it did not really go through. That is hypocrisy. The victims of violence are owed better by this government and by members of Parliament. We have to be honest and straightforward.
It is not easy to stand here and take the flak that is going around. I believe it is the truth, that this is a flawed bill, that it will get us into deeper legal morass, that there is a better way of doing it, and that the better way is the justice committee report itself which is legal, streamlined and the way to go.
If we were the government over there, in two months we would have a government bill and we would streamline this process. We would not engage in this hypocrisy.

The situation is sufficiently serious that this is at least a step forward and, if it is unconstitutional, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the member, we can try to take out any possible problems with unconstitutionality under the Charter of Rights. I would urge the member and his colleagues not to talk the bill out at 6.10 p.m. today, which is in about 20 minutes.
I would like to pay my respects to the member for Peterborough, to all of the members who have taken part
December 6, 1990

in this issue, and to the about 100,000 people who have signed petitions in favour of the principle of this bill.
I also would point out, although it has now gone by the boards, that the member for Peterborough asked each party to speak for 10 minutes and not longer today and then, by unanimous consent, we could have a vote. As an independent member, I will not speak for the full 10 minutes. I would simply make a plea to members of the New Democratic Party, because I think all other members here are agreed to let the bill go to committee, not to filibuster the proposal and I would give them three reasons. Earlier today we heard eloquent tributes in this House to the women who were killed in the tragedy at Ecole polytechnique in Montreal exactly a year ago today. How is it consistent for us in the same afternoon not to try to push this bill into committee, at the same we are all very distressed about what has happened in Montreal, across the country, and probably in every one of our constituencies?

Is it not better to push this bill into committee than to talk it out and say that we will bring in a better one next time?
I would point out to the members of the New Democratic Party that a recent New York Times article has estimated that there have been 250,000 homicides in the United States over the last 10 or 15 years. Would sending this bill to committee not speed up the day to come when people like the two people I am not to mention will find it harder to seek refuge in Canada, or sanctuary in Canada, than many have found it today?
Mr. Speaker, I might say as a former prosecutor of a number of homicide cases that there is now considerable dissymmetry between Canada and the United States, as I think the member for Scarborough-Rouge River pointed out. I recall a murder case in Alberta where the accused fled to California, her co-accused was tried in Fort McMurray. When she was found in California, as far as I can determine, the immigration authorities

simply put her on an airplane, told the RCMP in Vancouver when she would be landing, and she was arrested at the airport and brought back to Alberta for trial.

Mr. Speaker, I, and many others who value our Canadian agriculture industry, take strong objection to the answer of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to my question of November 22, 1990.
The minister took no time to refute recent editorials, consumer groups, and foreign governments which have been attacking supply management. He is leaving it to us

alone to set the record straight. Let's be truthful and get the facts straight.
Prior to the 1970s and the establishment of marketing boards in Canada, the dairy industry and prices of dairy products to consumers were continuously experiencing roller coaster highs and lows. Farmers could never rely on a stable income and the consumers' food budget was always fluctuating, creating financial instability for all concerned.
Economic policies based on the vicious laws of supply and demand are responsible for the surpluses and create the prices below the cost of production that we find in the United States and Europe. With no controls the market is flooded with surpluses and milk producers begin consistently to overproduce, creating huge stockpiles of butter, cheese, and non-fat dairy products.
Producers finally concluded that the only way for them to provide high quality products to consumers and achieve stability and a fair return for their labour and investment was to implement a production program to manage supply. Most importantly, our supply-managed system was implemented within international law, under Article XI of GATT.
Our dairy production is regulated to meet Canadian demand for dairy products, with adjustments for traditional imports and exports. Under supply management, the dairy industry produces a high quality product at a fair and reasonable price. Perhaps equally as important, Canada is now nearly self-sufficient in dairy products.
To say that dairy farmers are inefficient is a blatant lie. Since the introduction of supply management, milk yields have increased about 70 per cent in Canada, compared to 46 per cent in the U.S. and 31 per cent in New Zealand.
These groups continually talk about Canadian consumers being penalized by higher prices. Those who talk about the inefficiency of supply management neglect to mention that, while milk may be cheaper in the U.S. than in Canada, American milk is sold below the cost of production. U.S. producers are subsidized with tax dollars through surplus and herd buy-outs. The consumer pays in the end.
A popular conception by the media is that marketing boards and supply management systems are actually a form of subsidization. Supply management provides a
Adjournment Debate
fair return for producers from the marketplace without using huge amounts of taxpayers' dollars.
When supply management was first implemented under GATT, it was understood that subsidies were something that came out of the tax base.
Now the U.S. in particular is trying to argue that if consumers pay more than world price, that is a subsidy.
The GATT aggregate measure of support is a calculation used to qualify all government support programs for an industry and give these programs a monetary value. This calculation supposedly allows GATT to determine which support programs are trade distorting and which ones are not.
For the Canadian dairy industry, the AMS calculation considers both the domestic world price differential and the direct payment to producers. Such a calculation is misleading as the basis for 86 per cent of AMS calculation as it applies to the Canadian dairy industry is simply the difference between Canadian milk prices and world prices.
Such a calculation is irrelevant, and it is unfair because world prices reflect dumping by countries of the subsidized surplus production. The fact is that world prices are far below the actual production costs for most dairy producing countries.
The sensible marketing strategy these economic wizards appear to suggest is for our dairy farmers to produce huge surpluses below the cost of production. Yes, dairy producers and those who raise products under supply management in Canada have viable and successful operations, but does anyone ever stop to think of the huge investment they have had in their operations, or the 75-plus hours a week? They work milking cows twice a day like clockwork for 365 days a year.
It appears instead that these groups believe that dairy producers, and for that matter all farmers, do not deserve to earn a decent living for their families. Do they not have the right to a stable income? Do these groups expect them to accept a lower standard of living than other Canadians, living off the land?
Those agricultural sectors without supply management are continually plagued by boom and bust. Would these people like to have their salary go up and down like a yo-yo? The Department of Agriculture has predicted that farm incomes will fall by 25 per cent this year. What

Adjournment Debate
would these people do if their salaries were decreased by a quarter? How would they manage?
For that matter, how would we manage without a healthy food sector? On condemning supply management in our agricultural industry, these people all too often forget the importance of agriculture to our total economy.
recognize that supply management is a very important part of the Canadian long term agricultural policy.
I can assure everyone that the federal government is very committed to supply management, and that commitment is very firm. It is also clearly endorsed in our discussion paper Growing Together that we are all very familiar with.

For example, today there are some 35,000 dairy farmers in Canada. Each of these farmers supports two families; hence, there are some 70,000 farm families that depend on the dairy industry.
The supply management in Canada has been very highly successful in reducing market risk to producers, and I am sure the member agrees with that, preserving the family farm and ensuring that consumers have access to high quality food products at reasonable costs.
In addition, there are approximately 25,000 Canadians working in the dairy processing industry at nearly 400 plants located across this nation. The total number of people directly employed by the dairy industry is close to 100,000 Canadians, which represents approximately 14 per cent of the total aggregate business and employment.
Critics of supply management in agriculture forget that other sectors also have management of supply. Do you think General Motors or any other auto manufacturers produce an unlimited number of cars? What about subsidies and safety nets? If everything was based at world price and it is going to be considered a subsidy in agriculture, how long would it be before our social programs, old age pensions, CPP, OHIP, et cetera and other types of safety nets will also be considered as subsidies?
In conclusion, farmers are only asking for what other Canadians want, the right to earn a good living and support their families by hard work and struggling. We have built an agricultural industry that is envied the world over. We must not allow it to be destroyed.
