Mr. Speaker, I have stood in this place many times stating sobering statistics on violence against women, and here I am again tonight.
Tonight, let us forget the figures. Let us philosophize about a theme: the penalization of feminism. That is exactly what the Montreal massacre was about. It was about killing women who considered it natural to study a profession that interested them; women who did not realize that they would be physically punished for being feminists, unwitting feminists.
Like them, thousands of other Canadian women are punished for wanting self-sufficiency. Why did Chantal Daigle have to resort to wearing a disguise, sneaking out of the country and sleeping at a campground in order to access a medical service? Why, despite Supreme Court opinion, do Canadian women now face the possibility of being forced to reproduce by having to deal with doctors who could be branded criminals at someone else's whim? Why are women, who demand to exercise their own priorities, being in the words of a former chief justice, "profoundly interfered with"? Because these women are becoming too revealing. They are revealing their feminism. So, they seem to deserve punishment.
How bizarre it is that this government can criminalize a perfectly safe medical function and yet deliberately resist criminalizing the unwarranted possession of guns, whose prime function is to slaughter? One-third of these victims are women.
Why such blatant hypocrisy? Because, in each case women chose to choose, to practise feminism, something which unless punished enough, I suppose, might become a habit.
No wonder this government turns a blind eye to the lawmakers, interpreters, and enforcers who explain away violence against women by citing a number of things. They cite temporary loss of control, or work-related stress, or misunderstood signals from women, or my personal favourite, "She got what she asked for". Of course she did. She stood up for herself. She sought help. She fought back. She was a feminist. She was wrong. She had to be told.
Adjournment Debate
If feminism is so wrong in the eyes of this government, why bother reprimanding anti-feminists at all? Why bother giving three day sentences to confirmed wife batterers? I stand corrected. In some instances only a weekend sentence follows; the compassionate judge having made allowances for men who cannot miss their Friday night rituals. Mind you, I am not really complaining. Feminists have rituals, too. We have vigils. We call them vigils to help us remember those whom the judges forget.
Why even consider issuing demerit points, you know, the kind of demerit points that are issued to school yard bullies to university men who threaten their female colleagues with rape. Is it my mistake again, Mr. Speaker? In the University of B.C. case, none of the men has been officially sanctioned, nor are there signs of a formal inquiry in the works. Forgive me for suggesting that there should be. What can I say? Perhaps I want too much.
Why should we give so-called street women an economic break by allowing them to communicate the sale of their bodies in private? Or is once more my feminism leading me astray? To give credit where credit is due, this government has ensured that even those women who want out of prostitution will have problems finding decent work, thanks to their criminal records and a pitiful lack of reform programs.
The insults of women having to sneak around, sneak across the border for abortions; of prostitutes having to consider themselves outlaws except under the wink-wink, nudge-nudge circumstances; of women having to see their efforts undermined in a gun control bill whose very introduction came because of their efforts; of women having to get handcuffed to keep women's centres open; of women having to beg police officers to charge the accused, or plead with judges to sentence offenders adequately, and of women's votes being lured with hollow promises of a national child care program while domestic violence continues to dig the graves of Canadian women and children.
These realities contain two messages. First, that feminism has become such an integral part of the consciousness of Canadian women that it now threatens established power. If a threat cannot be destroyed, it must be disciplined. It must be punished.

The second message is that under this government the early 1990s are echoing the early 1890s, when the Criminal Code made birth control, and advising about birth control, illegal, and when etiquette manuals proclaimed that "women who overtax their vital energies by intellectual strain are self-made invalids and must accept the penalties of their position."
Penalizing feminism, Mr. Speaker, will not make it go away. It will only make it stronger. Female enrolment in engineering programs across Canada is higher than ever. Feminist resolve to amplify voices until government stops punishing them is greater than ever. The ultimate goal is clearer than ever: to liberate men as much as to liberate women so that "feminism" can be uttered by both sexes without anticipation of penalty.
This feminist will now await her penalty: three minutes of watching the government apologize first and give select information to puff up a pathetic record on action on violence against women.
Mr. Speaker, the penalty hardly suits the crime.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member realizes and recognizes that it is difficult to respond to all of her concerns in three minutes on the very delicate and very sincere situation and the concerns she has raised.
The government and the judiciary are keenly aware of the problem of judicial attitudes to issues such as gender equality and child sexual assault which may result in the making of ill-considered remarks. This was one of the reasons why the federal Minister of Justice of the day, along with his provincial and territorial counterparts, and the Canadian Judicial Counsel, agreed to establish the Canadian Judicial Centre in 1987.
One of its core functions is to respond to the educational requirements of both the federally and provincially appointed judiciary in Canada by designing judicial educational services to meet the requirements of the Canadian Judiciary and Skills Training, continuing professional education and professional enrichment.
The centre has become a central forum for the development of educational programs on gender equality for all levels of judges in this country. The centre is jointly funded by the federal, provincial and territorial
governments. The commitment of the federal government to the work of the centre is demonstrated by the fact that the level of financial support to the centre has recently been doubled.
The Minister of Justice considers the centre to be an appropriate body to assist the judiciary in developing a better appreciation of issues such as equality of the sexes, child abuse, and family violence, issues in which it has thus far shown considerable interest and concern.
The Canadian Judicial Council in conjunction with the Canadian Judicial Centre provided a course on gender equality at its 1990 summer seminar for federally appointed judges. This course was mandatory for those attending the seminar and focused on gender issues in the court room and in the application of the law.
Furthermore, the training seminar is given to all newly appointed judges and includes mandatory sessions dealing with gender issues. The Minister of Justice has called a National Conference on Women and the Law to be held in late 1991.
Continuing traditional education is an effective way of impressing upon members of the judiciary the need for the courts to reflect the changes in societal attitudes to gender issues, including child and spousal assault, which have occurred over the past few years.
With the increasing enrolment of women in law schools and especially with the presence of more women judges at all levels of court, attitudes are changing. Judges and law makers are more aware of women's concerns and more responsive to them. Indeed, with 81 women currently holding federal judicial office, including three members of the Supreme Court of Canada, the courts of every province and all the federally constituted courts are to an increasing extent being exposed to the presence and the views of women.

Mr. Speaker, everyone is familiar with the old adage that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. If one applies this adage to health care, I suppose one would say that preventing disease is better and less expensive than treating sick people. Yet as a society we spend billions on curing sick people and relatively little on preventing disease. This was the crux of the question which I raised in the House last Thursday and which I

had raised on previous occasions in June and earlier this fall.
The federal government spends $216 million on medical research, while it spends only $28 million on health care research which includes prevention of disease and health promotion. While the government spends relatively little on health care research, this is precisely the area that was cut by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in recent months.
In last year's budget, the minister was directed to reduce the expenditures of his department by $12 million. As was pointed out to me by one researcher, this amounts to 4-100ths of 1 per cent of the Department of National Health and Welfare's total budget of some $35 billion. As this researcher suggested to me, when one is asked to cut $12 million out of a budget of $35 billion or $40 billion, the largest budget of any department of the Government of Canada, surely there are ways that this could be done, surely there are ways that the pain could be spread around, rather than cutting the budget of the health care research program by some $4 million, which is what the minister chose to do.
The National Health Research and Development Program is the only funding source for applied health care research. It is the only funding source for areas of research such as cancer prevention, native health care, care for Alzheimer's sufferers, women's health care, health promotion, prevention of child sexual abuse, and prevention of family violence. Again I specify research into all these areas. Yet the minister reduced the budget of this program by $4 million and froze the budget for five years.
As a result of these cuts this fiscal year's competition was cancelled. In other words, no new projects will receive funding this year. And next year, when the competition is re-opened, the budget will be 13 per cent smaller.

To try and understand the impact of this cutback, Mr. Speaker, I recently spent some time meeting and listening to researchers involved in health care research. I met members of the interdisciplinary health research group at the Universite de Montreal. These people were doing research on emergency facilities. It is a known fact that crowded emergency wards are a problem that is very difficult to deal with. I met another researcher who is
Adjournment Debate
analysing decisive factors in the use of preventive services, such as the use of mammograms and Pap tests for cancer detection in women.
Mr. Speaker, many women do not take advantage of these tests. The point is to find out why and to convince them they should use these services.
Because of the cutbacks, these research projects have been postponed for one year, and researchers told me how negative the impact will be. Entire research teams will be lost because research assistants, doctorate-level students and programmers will decide to go on to something else, which means either working for the private sector or pursuing a career in medicine, which is more lucrative than research. Mr. Speaker, these cutbacks are also detrimental to the careers of researchers, since they are evaluated on productivity, the amounts of money they can raise and the number of articles they publish.

I spoke as well to a researcher from the University of Toronto who explained to me how two years ago many health care researchers underwent the difficult task of altering their areas of specialty to come into line with the government's stated priority at that time. The government sets up a program, people move into the field, they develop some expertise and then the government shuts off the funds. Research, this person told me, just does not work that way.
I am disappointed with the minister's reply to my question of why he chose to single out health care research for such harsh treatment. The minister said that this program is 55 per cent larger than it was in 1984.1 never said that he cut 100 per cent of the budget. I only asked him why he cut 13 per cent. That he has not explained.
I will conclude by saying that this sorry episode demonstrates two things: first, the need to restore the funding to this health care research program. I hope that somehow researchers in the field and members of Parliament can convince the minister to do so. Second, we have to give the national health research and development program an independent status similar to that of the other research councils so that cuts of this nature, which are very damaging to research, to health care in Canada and to the careers of researchers will not occur again.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say at the outset, there is no doubt that the federal government is strongly committed to funding health and medical research in this country.
The National Health Research and Development Program of the Department of National Health and Welfare plays a major role in the over-all federal effort, but the NHRDP is not the only federal funding source for health and medical research in Canada. Others include the Medical Research Council, the networks of Centres of Excellence Program, payments under clause 31 of Bill C-22 and other federal departments. Additionally, an extra $5 million is being provided in federal funds over five years to ensure the funding of an additional network addressing research problems related to seniors entirely in the research area normally supported by the NHRDP.
Furthermore, on Friday, November 30, 1990, the Deputy Minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare announced a new $2.5 million joint program with the Social Sciences and Humanities Research
Council to stimulate the creation of centres for health promotion research.
Since we came to office the NHRDP budget has increased by 55 per cent. It was this government that recognized the need for more research related to seniors, AIDS, alcohol and drugs, family violence and child sexual abuse. The number of projects and awards supported by the NHRDP has increased from 640 in 1985-86 to over 1,000 in 1989-90. Since April, over $8 million has been approved for new public health and health service research in addition to the $7 million study on Alzheimer's disease.
I would like to remind the hon. member since it may have escaped his notice that health services and public health research are alive and well in the Montreal area. As well, in the member's own riding $3 million, or more than 10 per cent of the current NHRDP budget is being spent this fiscal year.
